doc.title: Onaje Allan Gumbs interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2001

title: Woody Shaw as innovator and Carter Jefferson's tune
summary: He calls Shaw the last major trumpet innovator, notes his poor eyesight and democratic book, and praises Jefferson's Rise from Atlantis.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Trumpeters I admired: rating the horn players

blocks.x: But it was actually his liver or something. And so Carter died. And then not too long ago, Clinton, the bass player, it’s all the original Woody Shaw band, he passed away. So it was like Victor and I still holding up doing what we need to do individually. But that was one of the most incredible musical experiences, and to me Woody, and I’ll say this with no kind of censorship or any kind of limitations, Woody was probably the last major innovator on the trumpet. There are others who play now who are good. But as far as bringing a certain passion. Because his eyesight — you know a lot of times if someone has a certain kind of tragedy or a certain kind of situation as a musician it transfers into the music. And he being legally blind, which I know is something that really must have ate at him okay, I think it came out as passion in the music. And another thing that of course I have no idea of knowing but I think because of his eyesight being so bad, he couldn’t write tunes out a lot. So he relied on the band members to bring tunes to the book. So you had a very democratic situation, to the point that he would dog Carter to no end, because Carter wouldn’t put a tune into the book. He dogged him for about a year. And finally Carter brought this tune into the book. And we did a rehearsal at the Vanguard and I don’t know if you’ve ever had this experience but hearing a small group and in the small group you could actually hear the orchestra. Okay?
